overview: Czechia, also called the Czech Republic, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. Its capital, Prague, is known for its medieval old town and its castle. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into Czechia and Slovakia on 1 January 1993. Czechia joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.

geography.text: Czechia is made up of two main historic lands: Bohemia in the west, a basin ringed by low mountains, and Moravia in the east. The Vltava flows through Prague and joins the Elbe, which carries water north through Germany to the North Sea. The highest mountains are along the borders, including the Krkonoše range on the border with Poland.

history.text: Bohemia was a powerful kingdom in the Middle Ages, and under Charles IV Prague was the capital of the Holy Roman Empire. From 1526 the Czech lands were ruled by the Habsburgs. Czechoslovakia was created in 1918, occupied by Nazi Germany and then ruled by communists, until the peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989. In 1993 it split peacefully into two countries.

events.title: Charles University
events.text: The first university in central Europe is founded in Prague.

events.title: Defenestration of Prague
events.text: Officials are thrown from a castle window, sparking the Thirty Years' War.

events.title: Czechoslovakia founded
events.text: Czechs and Slovaks form a new country after the First World War.

events.title: Prague Spring
events.text: Reforms are crushed by a Soviet-led invasion.

events.title: Velvet Divorce
events.text: Czechoslovakia splits peacefully into Czechia and Slovakia.

government.text: Czechia is a parliamentary republic. The Chamber of Deputies, elected every four years, supports a government led by the Prime Minister. Since 2013 the President has been elected directly by the people. Czechia joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.

economy.text: Czechia has one of the strongest economies in central Europe, built on manufacturing. Cars are its biggest industry: Škoda, founded in 1895, makes cars there. Glass, beer and machinery are also important, and Prague is one of Europe's most visited cities.

culture.text: Prague's old centre, with its castle, Charles Bridge and astronomical clock, is one of the best-preserved in Europe. Czechs drink more beer per person than any other nation, and Pilsner lager was first brewed in Plzeň in 1842. The writer Franz Kafka and the composers Dvořák and Smetana all came from the Czech lands.

items.title: Prague Astronomical Clock
items.text: Running since 1410, one of the oldest working clocks of its kind.

items.title: Pilsner
items.text: The world's first pale lager, brewed in Plzeň in 1842.

items.title: The word 'robot'
items.text: Coined in a 1920 Czech play by Karel Čapek.

sport.text: Ice hockey and football are the most popular sports. Czech hockey players won Olympic gold in 1998, and the country has produced tennis stars such as Martina Navratilova and Petra Kvitová. The runner Emil Zátopek won three gold medals at the 1952 Olympics.

items.text: Olympic ice hockey gold at Nagano, beating Russia in the final.

items.title: Emil Zátopek
items.text: Won the 5,000 m, 10,000 m and marathon at the 1952 Olympics.

didYouKnow: Sugar cubes were invented in what is now Czechia, in 1843.
Czechia has more than 2,000 castles, chateaux and castle ruins.
